analysis.title: The Threshold, Not the Text: Why the AI Act's Economic Cost Will Be a Firm-Size Discontinuity and an Audit Vacuum, Not a Ceiling on Innovation
analysis.verdict: NomosX's position: the dominant public framing — "AI regulation versus innovation" — is novlangue. It conceals the two mechanisms that will actually determine the economic outcome, both of which are structural rather than substantive. The first is the discontinuity: tiered, threshold-triggered obligations generate a cliff at which firms rationally stop growing, stop reclassifying, and stop innovating. The single best-identified causal estimate available on this question is not about AI at all — it is the French administrative firm panel showing a sharp fall in the fraction of firms innovating just to the left of a size-contingent regulatory threshold, with reduced innovation responsiveness to exogenous demand shocks for firms below that threshold [SRC-91]. The AI Act is architecturally a size-and-tier-contingent regulation [SRC-83]. The mechanism ports. The second is the audit vacuum: the AI Act does not provide access to data for researchers and civil society, a regulatory gap in what would otherwise be a functioning third-party audit ecosystem [SRC-59]. A rule that cannot be independently verified does not produce trust; it produces documentation. This is the formalist trap that legal scholarship on the Brussels Effect routinely walks into — mistaking the diffusion of text for the diffusion of enforcement. The aggregate growth loss from AI regulation in Europe will be smaller than critics claim and the distributional loss larger than regulators admit. The reason is the shape of the AI-growth function: across 19 G20 countries from 2005 to 2023 using GMM with linear and quadratic terms, AI-related innovation has a positive and significant effect on economic growth, but the negative quadratic term confirms a concave relationship [SRC-40]. Concavity means the marginal social return to an additional unit of frontier AI capability is falling. If that is right, slowing the frontier by a few months costs less than is asserted — while blocking diffusion into the bottom of the firm distribution costs more. And diffusion is already the weak point: laggard firms in the bottom 40% of the productivity distribution converge toward the frontier more slowly in highly digital- and skill-intensive industries, indicating barriers to technology and knowledge diffusion [SRC-101]. Layer a threshold-contingent compliance regime on top of an already-broken diffusion channel and the result is not a slower frontier. It is a permanently thicker tail of non-adopters. The European market context sharpens the stakes rather than resolving them. The EU has lagged both quantitatively and qualitatively behind the US and China in growth over the last fifteen years while a new wave of high technology intensifies competition [SRC-55], and EU-funded AI investment during 2014–2020 — around EUR 8 billion at NUTS2 level — went disproportionately to more developed regions, generating spillovers that reinforce existing regional specialization [SRC-53]. Regulatory burden and public investment are therefore pushing in the same direction: toward concentration. Three qualifications bound this position. First, the causal identification is borrowed, not native: [SRC-91] concerns French labor regulation at a 50-employee threshold, not AI conformity assessment, and the transfer is an analogy grounded in mechanism rather than a replication. Second, no source in this evidence base quantifies AI Act compliance cost per firm; that number is non établie, and its absence is a fact about the research, not about the regulation. Third, the counter-mechanism is real: well-specified rules can enable markets rather than suppress them, and the evidence that regulatory frameworks in the EU, US and UK currently fail to confront the challenges of generative AI [SRC-14] cuts against the assumption that the status quo ante was innovation-optimal. Confidence: tempered, not firm.

trajectory.state: By 2030 the European AI market will be structurally bimodal. At the top, a small number of firms operating across all three major regulatory blocs will have internalised compliance as a standing function, absorbing the cost of divergent EU, US and Chinese priorities on transparency, fairness and privacy [SRC-6] and treating the AI Act's conformity regime as a barrier that protects their position rather than constrains it [SRC-98]. At the bottom, a thickening tail of firms will remain below classification triggers by design — restricting deployment scope, capping functionality, avoiding high-risk domains — reproducing at AI-tier boundaries the bunching already documented at labour-law size thresholds in France [SRC-91]. The middle thins. Three structural changes follow. First, an assurance industry consolidates. Responsible AI architecture, governance frameworks and regulatory convergence services move from consultancy offerings to standing enterprise functions [SRC-70]; certification labels become the consumer-facing interface of audit, tested against end-user comprehension rather than technical adequacy [SRC-49]; and in healthcare and finance the operative governance instrument is contractual — data usage agreements, master service provider contracts, indemnification clauses [SRC-16] — not statutory. Regulation is privatised at the point of application. Second, the audit ecosystem gap becomes politically salient. The absence of researcher and civil-society data access [SRC-59] will be exposed by the first serious enforcement failure in a high-risk domain. The most likely repair path is not statutory amendment but the construction of independent observation infrastructures, on the model by which citizen-generated data has been translated into evidence for shaping policy [SRC-58] and by which networks of citizen observatories increase the quality and quantity of independently generated monitoring data [SRC-84]. Expect proposals for an AI observatory network with legally mandated model access; expect industry to resist it more strongly than it resisted the Act itself, because access is the only obligation that cannot be satisfied on paper. Third, geoeconomic divergence hardens. Digital sovereignty discourse justifies state regulation and delimitation of data flows across very different contexts [SRC-80], and in the EU specifically it operates as regulatory mercantilism responding to perceived loss of competitiveness and dependence on foreign infrastructures [SRC-95]. Against a backdrop of fifteen years of EU underperformance relative to the US and China [SRC-55] and EU AI funding concentrated in already-developed regions [SRC-53], the political economy will push toward strategic exemptions, national champions and sandbox carve-outs — instruments that relieve the threshold pressure for selected firms while leaving it intact for everyone else, which worsens the distributional outcome while improving the headline one. Quantified expectation, stated as falsifiable: the AI Act's aggregate effect on EU GDP growth over this horizon will not be separately identifiable from macroeconomic noise, while firm-level microdata will show a statistically detectable discontinuity in AI deployment scope at tier boundaries. Both halves must hold for the position to stand.
trajectory.assumptions: Six conditions must hold. First, the AI Act's obligations must remain tier-triggered and discrete rather than being reworked into continuously scaling requirements; a continuous-obligation redesign would dissolve the threshold mechanism entirely. Second, the audit gap must persist — if the Commission legislates researcher and civil-society model access, the enforcement-vacuum branch collapses and the Brussels Effect strengthens rather than degrades [SRC-59]. Third, the concavity result must generalise beyond the G20 sample and the 2005–2023 window [SRC-40]; if AI proves to have increasing returns at current capability levels, frontier deceleration becomes far more costly and the position inverts. Fourth, diffusion barriers in digital- and skill-intensive industries must persist [SRC-101]; a genuine open-weights commoditisation of capable models would compress the fixed cost of adoption and could offset the compliance step, as the open-source versus closed-source deployment dilemma already suggests is contested [SRC-61]. Fifth, regulatory divergence between the EU, US and China must not converge; a binding international standard would eliminate the multiplier on fixed compliance cost [SRC-6]. Sixth, enforcement capacity must continue to lag market dynamics [SRC-98] — a well-resourced, technically competent enforcement apparatus applied symmetrically to large incumbents would neutralise the moat, though nothing in the evidence base indicates such capacity currently exists. If four or more of these fail, the trajectory should be discarded rather than adjusted.

causalChain.claim: The EU AI Act is a fundamental-rights instrument organised by risk tier, whose central ambition is the human-centric, ethical and responsible use of AI [SRC-83], and whose legal trustworthiness has been formally contested at proposal stage [SRC-86].
causalChain.warrant: A regulation whose operative classifications are normative categories (fundamental-rights risk) rather than measurable technical properties must be operationalised through classification thresholds. Threshold-based classification is the precondition for the discontinuity mechanism that follows.
causalChain.evidence: "The protection of fundamental rights, and the human-centric, ethical and responsible use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies in general, is a central ambition of European AI strategy" [SRC-83]. A dedicated legal response to the Commission's proposal for an Artificial Intelligence Act assesses how the EU can achieve legally trustworthy AI [SRC-86].

causalChain.claim: The AI Act, reviewed alongside the Digital Services Act for its treatment of third-party audits, does not provide access to data on models for researchers and civil society — an identified regulatory gap in the EU AI audit ecosystem [SRC-59].
causalChain.warrant: Third-party audit is the verification layer that converts a paper obligation into an enforceable norm. Absent independent data access, compliance is self-attested; self-attestation scales with legal-department capacity, not with actual system safety. This is the enforcement-gap blind spot that formalist legal analysis systematically misses.
causalChain.evidence: "We review to what extent third-party audits are part of both laws and how is access to information on models and the data provided... we identify a regulatory gap in that the AIA does not provide access to data for researchers and civil society" [SRC-59].

causalChain.claim: Comparative analysis of AI policy frameworks across the European Union, United States and China reveals significant variations in how these regions prioritise transparency, fairness and privacy, with substantial challenges to creating a unified standard [SRC-6], while digital sovereignty discourse drives state regulation and delimitation of data flows [SRC-80].
causalChain.warrant: Divergent substantive priorities across the three largest regulatory markets mean multinational compliance cost scales with the number of distinct regimes, not with the strictness of any one. Divergence is a multiplier on fixed compliance cost — and fixed costs are precisely what generate scale advantages.
causalChain.evidence: "A comparative analysis of international policy frameworks from regions including European Union, United States, China... results reveal significant variations in how global regions prioritize privacy, fairness, with challenges creating unified standard" [SRC-6]. "Approaches to state regulation and delimitation of data flows as well as programmes for national infrastructures are justified with calls to sovereignty across very different contexts" [SRC-80]. EU digital sovereignty discourse is explicitly framed around perceived loss of economic competitiveness and dependence on foreign infrastructures [SRC-95].

causalChain.claim: The fastest-growing AI investment sector globally lacks standardised implementation frameworks: financial institutions' AI expenditure is projected to double to USD 97 billion by 2027 at a 29.6 percent CAGR, yet the most notable persistent gap is the absence of standardised frameworks for AI implementation across financial sectors [SRC-8].
causalChain.warrant: Where capital is flowing fastest, the standard-setting deficit is largest. Absent standardisation, each firm must construct bespoke governance — a fixed cost invariant to firm size. Fixed cost invariant to size is the analytic definition of a scale barrier.
causalChain.evidence: "This rise in adoption is also evident in the projected doubling of financial institutions' AI expenditure, expected to reach $97 billion by 2027... With an estimated compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 29.6%, the financial sector is now the fastest-growing industry globally in terms of AI investment" and "persistent gaps remain, the most notable of which is the lack of standardized frameworks for AI implementation across financial sectors" [SRC-8].

causalChain.claim: The European economy has lagged the US and China in both quantitative and qualitative characteristics of growth over the last fifteen years while a new wave of high technology intensifies competition [SRC-55], and EU-funded AI investment of around EUR 8 billion in 2014–2020 concentrated in more developed regions [SRC-53].
causalChain.warrant: Public AI investment and private compliance capacity are correlated with regional development. Both instruments therefore push in the same direction — toward concentration in already-advantaged regions — rather than offsetting one another. Cohesion policy is not neutralising the regulatory concentration effect; it is amplifying it.
causalChain.evidence: "In the last 15 years, the European economy has been lagging in both the quantitative and qualitative characteristics of growth compared with its two main rivals" and "a new wave of high technology is intensifying EU's economic competition with the U.S. and China" [SRC-55]. "Around EUR 8 billion of EU funds were targeted for AI in regions. More developed regions have higher EU-funded investments. This generates spillover effects" [SRC-53].

causalChain.claim: Size-contingent regulation produces a measurable innovation discontinuity: in French population administrative firm panel data, there is a sharp fall in the fraction of firms innovating just to the left of the regulatory threshold, and below-threshold firms show reduced innovation response to exogenous demand shocks [SRC-91].
causalChain.warrant: The mechanism is anticipatory: firms forecast the discrete cost jump at the threshold and optimise below it, sacrificing growth-generating investment to avoid reclassification. The AI Act's tiered architecture [SRC-83] reproduces exactly this discrete-jump structure — obligations do not scale continuously with risk, they step at classification boundaries. Where costs step, firm behaviour bunches.
causalChain.evidence: "We build a tractable and quantifiable endogenous growth model with size-contingent regulations. We apply this to population administrative firm panel data from France, where many labor regulations bind at firms or more employees. Nonparametrically, we find that there is a sharp fall in the fraction of firms innovating just to the left of the regulatory threshold. Further, dynamic analysis shows a reduction in firm's response to exogenous demand shocks for firms below" [SRC-91].

causalChain.claim: Fixed compliance cost plus an enforcement apparatus that lags market dynamics converts regulation into an incumbency moat rather than a discipline on incumbents [SRC-98].
causalChain.warrant: Compliance has strong economies of scale: a legal, audit and documentation function is a near-fixed cost amortised over revenue. When enforcement additionally lags market dynamics, the largest firms capture a double advantage — they absorb the cost and they face the lowest probability of adverse enforcement. Add ownership-network incentives to soften competition [SRC-79] and the moat is structural, not incidental.
causalChain.evidence: Digital competition scholarship asks "how do we re-set the balance so that genuine innovation and choice prevail, all businesses have an equal opportunity to compete" and insists that "effective enforcement must keep pace with market dynamics" while calling for sensible and flexible rules [SRC-98]. Independently, general-equilibrium estimation over the universe of US public corporations finds that firms connected through common ownership networks face unilateral incentives to soften competition [SRC-79].

causalChain.claim: The compliance moat lands on an already-failing diffusion channel: laggard firms in the bottom 40 percent of the productivity distribution converge toward the frontier more slowly in highly digital- and skill-intensive industries, indicating barriers to technology and knowledge diffusion [SRC-101], while AI adoption itself exhibits epidemic diffusion in which early patterns establish path-dependencies [SRC-68].
causalChain.warrant: Diffusion, not invention, is where general-purpose technologies generate aggregate growth [SRC-50]. If regulation raises the fixed cost of adoption at the moment when adoption path-dependencies are being set [SRC-68], the damage is not a delayed frontier but a permanently wider adoption gap — a lock-in, not a lag.
causalChain.evidence: "Laggards are on average younger and smaller than more productive firms... Yet they converge at a slower rate in highly digital- and skill-intensive industries, [where] there are barriers to technology and knowledge diffusion" [SRC-101]. "Patterns related to early-stage diffusion establish path-dependencies which have implications for the distribution of technological opportunities and socio-economic returns linked to these technologies" [SRC-68].

causalChain.claim: The concavity of the AI-growth relationship makes frontier slowdown cheaper and diffusion failure more expensive than the standard debate assumes: AI-related innovation has a positive and significant effect on economic growth with a negative quadratic term confirming a concave relationship [SRC-40].
causalChain.warrant: Concavity implies diminishing marginal returns to additional AI intensity. The welfare-relevant question therefore shifts from "how fast is the frontier" to "how wide is the base". Regulation that trims the frontier while widening the base can be growth-positive; regulation that leaves the frontier untouched while narrowing the base is growth-negative regardless of how permissive it appears.
causalChain.evidence: "The linear model indicates that AI-related innovation has a positive and significant effect on economic growth, while the negative quadratic term confirms a concave relationship between AI and growth" across 19 G20 countries, 2005–2023, using GMM [SRC-40]. Independently, AI as a general-purpose technology "helps in the production, marketing, and customer acquisition of firms, increasing their productivity and consumer reach" [SRC-50].

causalChain.claim: The Act classifies by syndrome rather than by mechanism, reproducing a diagnostic error that other regulated sciences have already abandoned: critical care found that syndromic definitions must give way to subphenotypes because syndromes differentiate prognosis without differentiating treatment response [SRC-19].
causalChain.warrant: Risk tiers are syndromic categories: they bundle heterogeneous systems by application domain rather than by the mechanism that produces harm. Syndromic classification misallocates obligation — over-regulating benign systems inside a high-risk domain and under-regulating harmful ones outside it. The 'treatable traits' logic implies that harm-relevant properties (opacity, autonomy, feedback into consequential decisions) cross tier boundaries, which is why tier-based compliance produces cost without proportionate risk reduction.
causalChain.evidence: "Critical care uses syndromic definitions to describe patient groups... To impact clinical care, identification of subpopulations must do more than differentiate prognosis. It must differentiate response to treatment, ideally by defining subgroups with distinct functional or pathobiological mechanisms (endotypes)... the same treatment-responsive subpopulations may cross multiple clinical syndromes (treatable traits)" [SRC-19]. In parallel, regulatory toxicology finds that legislative frameworks must be adapted and that predictivity, reproducibility and quantification must be resolved before new methods including machine learning models can be broadly implemented [SRC-25].

causalChain.claim: Regulatory lag remains structural rather than resolved: generative AI diffusion created governance challenges including hallucination, jailbreaking, data training and validation issues, sensitive information leakage, opacity and control challenges [SRC-4], and institutions were forced to fill governance gaps in real time within six to eight months of ChatGPT's release, drawing on international soft-law instruments rather than scientific literature [SRC-9].
causalChain.warrant: When the rule-making cycle is slower than the technology cycle, the binding governance instrument becomes private and institutional soft law, not statute. This shifts the effective locus of AI regulation from parliaments to procurement contracts, university codes and vendor agreements [SRC-16] — a lex mercatoria of AI governance that operates below the level at which Regulatory Impact Assessment is conducted.
causalChain.evidence: "The rapid and widespread diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has unlocked new capabilities... underscores its key risks, including hallucination, jailbreaking, data training and validation issues, sensitive information leakage, opacity, control challenges, design and implementation risks" [SRC-4]. Thirty leading universities from the Shanghai Ranking top 500 issued first-generation AI policies within six to eight months, "grounded in publicly available ethical norms/guidelines of international organisations... not in scientific literature" [SRC-9]; a parallel global study across six regions finds persistent gaps in institutional frameworks, particularly data privacy and equitable access [SRC-11].

causalChain.claim: By 2028, the observable signature of AI regulation in European firm data will be bunching at classification boundaries — firms declining to reclassify systems upward, restricting deployment scope, or capping user numbers to remain below tier triggers — rather than an economy-wide fall in AI investment.
causalChain.warrant: Firms optimise against discrete cost steps by avoiding the step, not by exiting the market. The behavioural response to threshold regulation is scope restriction and classification avoidance, which is invisible in aggregate R&D statistics but visible in the distribution of firm size and in the declared risk classification of deployed systems.
causalChain.evidence: Derived from the threshold mechanism: French administrative panel data show a sharp fall in the fraction of firms innovating just left of a size-contingent regulatory threshold, with reduced dynamic response to demand shocks below it [SRC-91].

causalChain.claim: The Brussels Effect will replicate in documentation but degrade in enforcement: third countries and multinationals will adopt EU-style conformity documentation without adopting EU-level verification, producing convergence of paperwork and divergence of practice.
causalChain.warrant: Norm export via market access requires that compliance be observable to the exporting regulator. Where verification depends on self-attestation, the cheapest compliance strategy for a foreign firm is to reproduce the document template without reproducing the internal control. The Brussels Effect is a function of enforcement reach, not of legislative ambition — which is why GDPR's diffusion cannot be assumed to repeat.
causalChain.evidence: Derived from the audit gap: the AI Act does not provide access to data for researchers and civil society, identified as a regulatory gap in the intended EU AI audit ecosystem [SRC-59].

causalChain.claim: A durable assurance layer will form between AI developers and deployers — certification, audit, model documentation and governance architecture — capturing a rising share of AI-related value while contributing little to frontier capability.
causalChain.warrant: When verification is mandatory but non-standardised [SRC-8], intermediaries arise to supply verification as a service. The assurance layer is rent extracted from the compliance obligation; it is a real industry with real employment, and it is not the same thing as innovation in capability. Conflating the two is how regulators will claim the Act was innovation-neutral.
causalChain.evidence: Derived from the compliance-moat mechanism and its institutional response: responsible AI architecture in enterprise modernisation now explicitly combines governance frameworks, equity implications and regulatory convergence as a distinct practice area [SRC-70]; empirical mixed-method work on certification labels for trustworthy AI (interviews N=12, census-representative survey N=302) investigates labels as a solution to communicating audit outcomes to end-users [SRC-49]; healthcare deployment already runs through business associate agreements, data usage agreements and master service provider contracts specifying processing, liability, notification and indemnification [SRC-16].

causalChain.claim: Aggregate EU growth loss attributable to the AI Act will be modest and difficult to identify statistically; the distributional loss — concentrated in SMEs, laggard firms and less-developed regions — will be larger and will be misread as a general innovation slowdown.
causalChain.warrant: Concavity caps the aggregate loss from frontier deceleration while diffusion barriers uncap the distributional loss from adoption failure. Because national accounts aggregate, the distributional damage appears in the data only with a lag and only in firm-level microdata — creating a measurement asymmetry that will sustain the false 'regulation versus innovation' debate for years after it should have ended.
causalChain.evidence: Derived from the concavity mechanism [SRC-40] combined with the diffusion barrier: laggards in the bottom 40 percent of the productivity distribution converge more slowly in digital- and skill-intensive industries [SRC-101], and generative AI's productivity and job-creation benefits "will likely be distributed unevenly" [SRC-14].

keyFindings: The only causally identified evidence on regulation and innovation in this base is a firm-size discontinuity: French population administrative panel data show a sharp fall in the fraction of firms innovating just left of a size-contingent regulatory threshold, plus reduced innovation response to exogenous demand shocks below it [SRC-91]. The AI Act's tiered architecture [SRC-83] reproduces the discrete-cost-step structure that generates this effect.

The AI Act does not provide access to data for researchers and civil society, an explicit regulatory gap in the intended EU AI audit ecosystem [SRC-59]. Without independent verification, compliance is self-attested, the Brussels Effect exports documentation rather than enforcement, and effective enforcement fails to keep pace with market dynamics in exactly the way digital competition scholarship warns against [SRC-98].

The AI-growth relationship is concave: across 19 G20 economies from 2005 to 2023, AI-related innovation has a positive and significant linear effect while the negative quadratic term confirms diminishing returns [SRC-40]. Concavity implies that frontier deceleration is cheaper than commonly claimed and adoption failure is more expensive — and adoption is already failing, with bottom-40-percent laggard firms converging more slowly precisely in digital- and skill-intensive industries [SRC-101].

Regulatory divergence, not regulatory strictness, is the cost multiplier. Comparative analysis of EU, US and Chinese frameworks finds significant variation in how transparency, fairness and privacy are prioritised, with substantive obstacles to a unified standard [SRC-6], while digital sovereignty discourse justifies state delimitation of data flows across contexts [SRC-80] and functions in the EU as regulatory mercantilism responding to competitiveness loss [SRC-95].

The compliance obligation is producing a distinct assurance industry rather than suppressing AI activity: responsible AI architecture now combines governance frameworks with regulatory convergence as a standing enterprise function [SRC-70], certification labels are being empirically tested on end-users (N=12 interviews, 302-person census-representative survey) [SRC-49], and financial-sector AI spend is projected to double to USD 97 billion by 2027 at 29.6 percent CAGR despite the absence of standardised implementation frameworks [SRC-8]. Value migrating to the compliance layer will be misreported as regulation being innovation-neutral.
analysis.throughLine: The AI Act's measurable growth cost will come not from the strictness of its obligations but from tier and size thresholds that make firms stop growing, compounded by an audit vacuum that exports documentation instead of trust.

signals: Distribution of declared risk classifications in EU conformity filings: bunching immediately below high-risk tier triggers would confirm the threshold mechanism [SRC-91]; a smooth distribution would falsify it.

Whether the Commission or Parliament legislates researcher and civil-society access to model and training data, closing the identified audit-ecosystem gap [SRC-59] — the single highest-information regulatory event in this horizon.

Growth of dedicated responsible-AI governance functions inside non-technology enterprises, distinguishable from capability R&D spend [SRC-70], and adoption rates of end-user-facing certification labels [SRC-49].

Whether financial-sector AI expenditure tracks the projected doubling to USD 97 billion by 2027 at 29.6 percent CAGR [SRC-8], and whether the sector converges on standardised implementation frameworks or remains fragmented.

Convergence or further divergence in how the EU, US and China prioritise transparency, fairness and privacy [SRC-6], including whether NIST-process stakeholder contestation resolves toward EU-compatible obligations [SRC-35].
SME participation and graduation rates in EU AI regulatory sandboxes — currently non établie in this evidence base and the most consequential missing measurement.
Productivity convergence rates for bottom-40-percent laggard firms in digital- and skill-intensive industries [SRC-101]: continued divergence confirms the diffusion-failure amplification.
Whether open-weight model performance continues closing on closed-source performance, which would compress adoption fixed costs and blunt the threshold effect [SRC-61].

Realisation of large sectoral efficiency gains where they are quantifiable — for example whether AI adoption in healthcare approaches the estimated 5–10 percent of national spending, USD 200–360 billion annually in the US [SRC-54] — and whether EU health systems capture a comparable share.

Regional concentration of EU-funded AI investment in the post-2020 programming period relative to the roughly EUR 8 billion NUTS2 pattern of 2014–2020 [SRC-53]; further concentration confirms that cohesion instruments are amplifying rather than offsetting regulatory concentration.

Emergence of independent AI monitoring infrastructures modelled on citizen observatory networks with mandated data access [SRC-58][SRC-84], and industry resistance intensity as a proxy for how binding such access would actually be.

Shift of effective governance into contractual instruments — data usage agreements, master service provider contracts, indemnification clauses [SRC-16] — indicating that statutory regulation is being displaced by a private lex mercatoria operating below the level at which impact assessment occurs.
whatToWatch.horizonCheck: Revisit no later than 1 October 2027, and immediately upon any of three triggers: publication of the first cross-member-state dataset on AI Act risk-tier classifications; a legislative proposal on researcher data access to AI models; or the first enforcement action against a major provider in a high-risk domain. A shorter interim check in Q2 2027 is warranted if EU sandbox participation data are published, since that is currently the largest single measurement gap in the argument.
whatToWatch.whatWouldChangeMind: Four falsifiers, in order of force. First: firm-level microdata showing no discontinuity in AI system classification, deployment scope or firm growth at AI Act tier boundaries by end-2028. That is the direct test of the ported threshold mechanism [SRC-91], and its failure collapses the central claim. Second: replication studies overturning the concave AI-growth relationship [SRC-40] and establishing increasing returns at current capability levels — in which case frontier deceleration dominates diffusion failure and the whole cost accounting inverts. Third: enactment and enforcement of mandatory third-party model and data access closing the audit gap [SRC-59], which would convert the AI Act from a documentation regime into a verification regime, restore the Brussels Effect, and make the compliance moat contestable. Fourth: evidence that regulatory sandboxes deliver measurable SME time-to-market reduction at scale, which would show the threshold pressure is being relieved precisely where it binds hardest. Any one of the first three would require substantial revision; the first two would require abandonment.

analysis.anchoringBasis: Four anchors carry this analysis, and they differ in evidential weight. The strongest is quasi-experimental. A tractable, quantifiable endogenous growth model applied to population administrative firm panel data from France — where many labor regulations bind at 50 or more employees — finds nonparametrically a sharp fall in the fraction of firms innovating just to the left of the regulatory threshold, and a dynamic reduction in firms' innovation response to exogenous demand shocks below the threshold [SRC-91]. This is the only source in the base offering credible causal identification of regulation's effect on innovation. The second is textual and institutional. The protection of fundamental rights and the human-centric, ethical and responsible use of AI is the central ambition of European AI strategy [SRC-83]; the Commission's proposal has been assessed against the standard of legally trustworthy AI and found wanting on specific counts [SRC-86]; and the Act, alongside the Digital Services Act, does not provide access to information on models and data for researchers and civil society, which constitutes an identified regulatory gap in the intended audit ecosystem [SRC-59]. Enforcement capability, not obligation stringency, is the binding variable — a point reinforced by the observation from digital competition scholarship that effective enforcement must keep pace with market dynamics if genuine innovation and choice are to prevail [SRC-98]. The third is the growth function itself. AI-related innovation has a positive and significant effect on economic growth in G20 economies, with a negative quadratic term confirming concavity [SRC-40]; AI functions as a general-purpose technology aiding production, marketing and customer acquisition, increasing firm productivity and consumer reach [SRC-50]; and in China, 20,178 firm-year observations from 2007–2022 show AI innovation operating through governance-mediated affordance actualisation in high-growth firms [SRC-29]. Sector-level magnitudes exist where costs are measurable: wider AI adoption in US healthcare could yield savings of 5–10 percent of national health spending, roughly USD 200–360 billion annually [SRC-54]; financial institutions' AI expenditure is projected to double to USD 97 billion by 2027 at a 29.6 percent CAGR [SRC-8]. The fourth is diffusion. Laggard firms in the bottom 40 percent of the productivity distribution converge more slowly toward the frontier precisely in digital- and skill-intensive industries [SRC-101], while AI adoption itself exhibits epidemic diffusion properties in which early-stage patterns establish path-dependencies shaping the distribution of technological opportunity and socio-economic returns [SRC-68]. The threshold mechanism and the diffusion mechanism compound.

gaps: No source in this base quantifies AI Act compliance cost per firm, per risk tier, or as a share of R&D spend. This number is non établie. Every claim about the magnitude of the compliance burden — including this analysis's — is therefore directional, not quantified.

No source measures EU regulatory sandbox throughput, SME participation, graduation-to-deployment rates, or time-to-market effects. The second-largest mechanism in the Pass 1 friction map is empirically unobserved.

No firm-level data on AI system classification decisions under the Act exist yet, which means the central prediction of this analysis — bunching at tier boundaries — is currently untestable and will remain so until conformity filing data are published.

The benefit side of the Regulatory Impact Assessment is systematically unmeasured. Standardised metrics for the burden of information harms are themselves identified as absent, requiring a common vocabulary, evidence review and technical working group before quantification is possible [SRC-26]; the same measurement problem applies to avoided algorithmic discrimination and preserved due process.

No source establishes whether explainability requirements impose a genuine performance cost. The healthcare explainability literature frames the question as medical, legal, ethical and societal rather than purely technological [SRC-74], and evaluation metrics for generative healthcare systems are proposed but not yet implemented, validated or benchmarked [SRC-10]. The transparency-performance trade-off is asserted more often than it is measured.

The analytic-perspective problem is unresolved and consequential. Health economics establishes that the choice of perspective directly influences which costs enter the numerator, and that broadening the perspective can either decrease or increase the resulting ratio depending on context [SRC-7]. Applied to AI regulation: whether the Act 'costs' growth depends entirely on whose costs are counted — developer, deployer, worker, or society. No AI Regulatory Impact Assessment in this base states its perspective explicitly.

Enforcement capacity data are absent. Formalist analysis of statutory text tells us nothing about member-state notified-body capacity, technical competence, or willingness to act against large providers — the variable on which the compliance-moat mechanism most depends [SRC-98].

Labour-market transmission is under-evidenced. Automation is characterised as labour-saving, resource-saving and productive of winner-takes-all dynamics [SRC-73], and generative AI's workplace benefits are expected to be unevenly distributed [SRC-14], but no source in this base links AI regulation specifically to employment outcomes.

The offshored data-work layer that underpins AI supply chains — procured via arm's-length contracts and marketplace platforms across France, Madagascar and Venezuela [SRC-57] — falls almost entirely outside the AI Act's territorial and substantive scope. The regulation governs deployment while the labour and extraction occur elsewhere; this asymmetry is unquantified and structurally important.
evidenceAssessment.weakestLink: Link 10, the syndromic-classification critique via critical-care subphenotyping [SRC-19]. This is a cross-domain analogy, not evidence. Nothing in [SRC-19] concerns AI regulation, and nothing in the AI sources establishes that tier-based classification misallocates obligation relative to actual harm mechanism. The analogy is intellectually productive — it names a real design property of the Act's architecture [SRC-83] and is loosely supported by the parallel finding in regulatory toxicology that predictivity, reproducibility and quantification must be resolved before new methodologies including machine learning models can be regulatorily implemented [SRC-25] — but it does not carry evidential weight and should not be cited as if it did. A reader who rejects link 10 entirely loses nothing from links 6 through 9, which is why the chain is constructed so that the core does not depend on it.
strongestLinks: Link 6 (threshold discontinuity). This is the only causally identified estimate of regulation's effect on innovation in the entire evidence base: population administrative firm panel data from France, nonparametric identification of a sharp fall in the innovating fraction just left of a size-contingent threshold, plus a dynamic reduction in innovation response to demand shocks below it [SRC-91]. The identification is strong; the transfer to AI is an argument by mechanism, not a replication.

Link 2 (audit vacuum). A direct, specific textual finding from legal analysis of both the DSA and the AIA: the AIA does not provide access to data for researchers and civil society, identified as a regulatory gap in the intended EU AI audit ecosystem [SRC-59]. This is a fact about the instrument, not an inference about behaviour, and it is corroborated by the independent observation that effective enforcement must keep pace with market dynamics [SRC-98].

Link 9 (concavity). A GMM estimation over 19 G20 countries spanning 2005–2023 with explicit linear and quadratic specification, finding a positive linear and negative quadratic AI-growth relation [SRC-40], consistent with the general-purpose-technology framing in independent panel work [SRC-50]. Single-study, but methodologically specified and directly on point.

Link 8 (diffusion failure). Cross-country firm-level evidence that laggards in the bottom 40 percent of the productivity distribution converge more slowly precisely in digital- and skill-intensive industries [SRC-101], independently corroborated by transformer-based firm-level measurement of AI adoption showing epidemic diffusion with path-dependent early patterns [SRC-68]. Two methodologically distinct sources converge on the same structural fact.
evidenceAssessment.sourceDiversity: The evidence base is broad in provider terms and badly skewed in topical terms, and this must be stated plainly rather than glossed. Providers span OpenAlex, NBER, OECD, WHO-GHO, World Bank, INRIA, ETH Zurich, Max Planck, Semantic Scholar, OpenReview, CORDIS, Eurostat, UN, JSTOR, IMF, EuropePMC, bioRxiv and others — well beyond the seven-provider threshold. Topically, however, a large share of the highest-quality sources concern health, climate and biomedical research and are irrelevant or only analogically relevant to AI regulation's economic effects. The consequential imbalance is this: roughly a dozen sources speak directly to AI regulation and economics, and only one — [SRC-91] — offers credible causal identification, and it concerns French labour law rather than AI. The strongest empirical AI-growth evidence is geographically displaced from the regulatory question: the G20 panel [SRC-40], the Chinese 20,178 firm-year study of AI innovation and high-growth firms under governance [SRC-29], the Chinese green-growth study in the Huaihe River Basin [SRC-31], and the Indian renewable-energy AI study using Dynamic ARDL over 1987–2020 [SRC-56] all measure AI-growth relationships outside the EU regulatory environment. The legal sources are predominantly European and predominantly normative, carrying the pro-regulation bias endemic to academic legal literature; the economic sources are predominantly American and carry the opposite prior. This analysis attempts to hold both. Jurisdictional bias is partially but not fully controlled. Comparative EU/US/China framework analysis [SRC-6], digital sovereignty scholarship [SRC-80][SRC-95], and Kazakhstan-focused ethical-legal analysis of AI in innovation activity [SRC-39] provide some non-EU legal perspective, and the global-health governance material introduces Global South framing including explicit attention to power imbalances and digital colonialism in AI research partnerships across 31 countries [SRC-18]. But there is no African, Latin American or South Asian regulatory-economic source, and the AI data-work supply chain reaching Madagascar and Venezuela [SRC-57] appears only as a labour-geography observation, not as a regulatory analysis. Evidence-quality caution is warranted across the digital-policy literature generally. In an adjacent domain, 72 percent of systematic reviews on digital interventions were rated critically low quality against only 2 percent high quality [SRC-22]; in climate-health research, only 5 percent of 511 included papers considered adaptation strategies at all [SRC-23]. Both indicate a general pattern in fast-moving policy-relevant fields: high publication volume, low methodological quality, and systematic under-attention to implementation. The AI governance literature — with generative AI ethics reviews synthesising as few as 37 studies [SRC-12] and institutional policy studies drawing on 30 universities [SRC-9] or six regions [SRC-11] — shows the same signature. Confidence should be adjusted downward accordingly, and has been.

rejectedAlternatives.scenario: Strong Brussels Effect: the AI Act becomes the de facto global standard, as GDPR did, producing a race to the top in AI governance and a first-mover advantage for compliant European firms.
rejectedAlternatives.whyRejected: The GDPR analogy assumes verification capability that the AI Act lacks: it does not provide access to data for researchers and civil society, an explicit regulatory gap in the intended audit ecosystem [SRC-59]. Comparative analysis of EU, US and Chinese frameworks shows significant divergence in how privacy and fairness are prioritised, with substantive challenges to any unified standard [SRC-6], and digital sovereignty discourse across jurisdictions justifies delimitation of data flows rather than harmonisation [SRC-80]. Norm export requires observability; self-attested compliance exports templates.
rejectedAlternatives.residualRisk: If a major non-EU jurisdiction adopts EU-equivalent conformity assessment with independent audit — plausible given that public standards processes are already sites of contested stakeholder definition of alignment obligations [SRC-35] — then EU firms gain a genuine first-mover position and the concentration cost is offset by export advantage. This scenario is under-weighted here and should be revisited if formal mutual-recognition negotiations begin.

rejectedAlternatives.scenario: Regulatory sandboxes materially offset the compliance burden, allowing SMEs to test under relaxed oversight and reach market at speed comparable to unregulated jurisdictions.
rejectedAlternatives.whyRejected: The evidence base contains no measurement of sandbox throughput, graduation rates, or effect on time-to-market. The available material speaks to ambition — the EU positioning itself as an ethics trailblazer developing guidance for new and emerging technologies [SRC-1] — not to outcomes. Pass 2 assessed this mechanism as cracked and non-extrapolable. Sandboxes also allocate discretionary relief, which by construction advantages firms with the administrative capacity to apply, reproducing rather than correcting the size gradient.
rejectedAlternatives.residualRisk: If sandbox participation data show high SME throughput and measurable time-to-market reduction, the threshold discontinuity could be substantially blunted at the point where it matters most. The absence of such data is currently a research gap, not evidence of failure — a distinction that must be preserved.

rejectedAlternatives.scenario: Regulation is essentially irrelevant: AI investment is driven by capability, talent and capital availability, and firms invest regardless of regulatory uncertainty.
rejectedAlternatives.whyRejected: Asymmetric adoption of AI across industries is already attributed to varying regulatory pressures and institutional constraints, with the risk of economic disruption arriving before societal understanding [SRC-48]. The French threshold evidence shows firms demonstrably altering innovation behaviour in anticipation of a discrete regulatory cost, including reduced responsiveness to demand shocks [SRC-91]. Regulation is not a binary on-off switch on investment; it is a shaper of where investment lands in the firm-size distribution, which is precisely the effect this analysis isolates.
rejectedAlternatives.residualRisk: If AI capability commoditises fast enough that compliance cost becomes negligible relative to deployment value — a live possibility given open-source models catching up with closed-source performance [SRC-61] — the threshold effect could be swamped. This is the single most plausible route by which the whole position becomes irrelevant rather than wrong.

rejectedAlternatives.scenario: Regulation stifles innovation outright: the AI Act produces a measurable, economy-wide reduction in EU AI investment and a visible transatlantic capability gap attributable to law.
rejectedAlternatives.whyRejected: This is the position the evidence least supports. The AI-growth relationship is concave [SRC-40], meaning marginal frontier capability yields diminishing growth returns, so even a real frontier deceleration produces a small aggregate effect. Europe's growth underperformance relative to the US and China predates the AI Act by roughly fifteen years and is documented as both quantitative and qualitative [SRC-55], with structural causes including regional concentration of investment [SRC-53] and slow technology diffusion to laggard firms [SRC-101]. Attributing a pre-existing structural gap to a recent statute is a category error that serves lobbying, not analysis.
rejectedAlternatives.residualRisk: If frontier AI turns out to exhibit increasing rather than diminishing returns at current capability levels, a modest frontier delay compounds into a large gap and this rejection is wrong. The concavity finding rests on a single GMM study of 19 countries [SRC-40] and has not been replicated in the evidence base.

rejectedAlternatives.scenario: Regulation redistributes AI's economic gains toward consumers and workers, producing more inclusive growth that compensates for any innovation cost.
rejectedAlternatives.whyRejected: Pass 2 assessed this as cracked, and the evidence base supports the assessment. Generative AI can both exacerbate and ameliorate socioeconomic inequalities, and existing policy frameworks in the EU, US and UK are found to fail to fully confront the identified challenges [SRC-14]. Automation technologies are characterised as labour-saving, resource-saving and productive of winner-takes-all dynamics that advantage developed countries [SRC-73]. Transparency and data-protection obligations impose costs; no source in this base demonstrates that those costs translate into measured gains for consumers or workers.
rejectedAlternatives.residualRisk: Redistribution may operate through channels not measured here — reduced discriminatory harm, avoided misinformation costs, preserved due process. The absence of measurement is severe: standardised metrics for the burden of information harms are themselves identified as missing and in need of a common vocabulary and technical working group [SRC-26]. Costs are counted; benefits are not. That asymmetry systematically biases every Regulatory Impact Assessment in this domain against regulation.
